t: Maximize Alternating Sum Using Swaps — Editorial
o: The swaps define an undirected graph on indices. Since any transposition is allowed repeatedly, all elements within one connected component can be rearranged into **any** permutation of that component's multiset (transpositions generate the full symmetric group). Elements never leave their component. The alternating sum adds values at even indices and subtracts values at odd indices, so within each component we should place the largest values on the component's even-index slots and the smallest on its odd-index slots. In Example 1, indices {0,1,2} form one component with 2 even slots, so we put the two largest (3,2) at even positions: 3-1+2=4. In Example 2, index 0 is isolated so nums[0]=1 stays fixed, while {1,2} can be permuted but both contribute -x+x=0 either way, giving 1-2+3=2. With n up to 1e5 we need near-linear grouping plus sorting.
k: Swaps are transpositions, so each connected component of the swap graph can realize every permutation of its own elements — components are closed sets.
Within a component with e even-index slots, greedily assign the e largest values to those slots to maximize (+larges) − (smalls).
Grouping via Union-Find or DFS/BFS over swaps, then per-component sorting, yields O(n log n) overall.

a.n: Approach 1: DFS Components + Per-Component Greedy Sort
a.i: Build the graph from swaps, find connected components with DFS/BFS, then for each component collect its values and count how many even indices it contains. Sorting the component's values descending and assigning the first `e` values (with + sign) and the rest (with − sign) is optimal by an exchange argument: swapping any larger value into a + slot and smaller into a − slot never decreases the sum.
s: DFS/BFS to label each index with a component id.
For each component, gather values and count even indices e.
Sort values descending; add the first e with + sign, remaining with − sign.
a.t: O(n log n) — building the graph and DFS are O(n + m), and sorting each component's values totals O(n log n).
a.sp: O(n + m) — adjacency lists, component labels, and DFS stack.

a.i: Same greedy assignment, but components are found with Union-Find instead of graph traversal. Union pi and qi for every swap, then bucket values by root. This avoids explicit adjacency lists and is typically faster and simpler in practice; correctness follows from the same exchange argument.
s: Initialize DSU over n indices; union endpoints of each swap.
For each index, append its value to the group keyed by find(i), counting even indices per group.
Add top e values positively and the rest negatively per group.
a.t: O(n log n + m α(n)) — DSU operations are nearly constant; sorting all grouped values dominates.
a.sp: O(n) — DSU array and grouped value buckets.

w: In an interview, lead with the observation that transpositions generate full permutations inside each connected component — this reframes the problem as pure assignment. Then present the Union-Find solution as the final answer since it is shortest and fastest; mention DFS as an equivalent alternative. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a component may have unequal counts of even/odd slots (the split point differs per component), using 32-bit integers (sums reach ~1e14), and assuming swaps must be applied exactly once rather than any number of times. Edge cases: empty swaps (answer is just the original alternating sum), duplicate values, and a single giant component. Follow-ups might ask for the minimum number of swaps to achieve the optimum, or handling directed/constrained swaps where only some permutations are reachable.
